utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. To continue with the evidence of 6D-2 we require to go straight into closed session. 8 [Closed session] [Confidentiality partly lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the outset of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Yesterday we were looking at Exhibit 6D66 [sic] and now I would like to look at a related document you looked at before, this is 6D778, this was a telegram, I believe, dated the 15th of April, 1999. Do you have a copy of that one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I've just found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this one is from General Lukic to all the chiefs of the SUPs in Kosovo and the PJP commanders of Detachments 21 to 87. And it says: "Even though an order was issued on the fifth day of April to prevent civilians from leaving ..." I think you told us yesterday you thought this reflects that there was an error in that other document that's dated the 3rd of April and it probably should have been the 5th of April on Exhibit 6D666; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to this document that's the way it would look, although I don't see how that happened. Perhaps there is a mistake in the date here in the Telex or over there. I really could not be of assistance on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one reason I have a question about whether or not this document relates to that official note we saw in 6D666 is that this one is addressed to the PJP commanders and that official note, we can look at it if you need to, but that official note appeared to be only referring to an order that had gone to the SUP chiefs. Would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this doesn't really confuse me. My understanding is that the detachment commanders were under the chiefs of SUPs then, under their sort of command or something like that, that's my understanding. That is my understanding of why only the chiefs were told originally and now the others were added, I don't know why, but I assume that the chiefs of the SUPs at those meetings transmitted that to us and to the commanders of the detachments. That is how I would understand the previous as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this telegram, is this the original or where does this copy come from, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I could remember something like that. I remember it as a document, but where it comes from -- I mean well this is a copy of this

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What can you tell us about authenticity? I see what appears to be a handwritten number 9 in the upper right-hand corner on the Serbian version, but there's no signature, there's no stamp. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I said that I do have an inclination towards these documents, they are verifiable, there is a code down here that can be seen, the last four lines, the first line. And if you look at that code you can identify the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where would that code be found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this distribution centre that functioned then in the log-books that are kept, that is to say -- well, to put it in very simple terms there is this Telex service or these teleprinter operators in a particular service that send these dispatches out. So perhaps you could find it there -- well, most probably. That is why I said that the dispatch could be identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I know in connection with some of our VJ documents we saw some log-books of in-going and out-going telegrams that sometimes had handwritten entries showing what telegram had been sent and when and by whom, et cetera. Were those similar to what the MUP had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to have a look at those documents, then I could say. I cannot really help you very much on that because I was never involved in that line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Let's move to another document that you saw before, this is Exhibit P1996. These are the minutes of a meeting at the MUP staff in Pristina on the 7th of May. I think Mr. Lukic asked you about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before moving on --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- your explanation, Witness, for seeing no inconsistency between this document and the earlier one was your understanding that the PJP detachment commanders came under the SUP chiefs. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I misspoke. They took part in these meetings, the collegium meetings of the chief of SUP, and I believe that then they were familiarized with the previous order, just as I was. It is in that sense that I explained that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the collegium meetings they attended, were they the meetings in the area to which they had been sent or the collegium meetings in their home SUP area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And where did his -- what was his normal home base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he hailed from Nis, that is what I heard, he himself but I'm not sure that his detachment was from the Nis SUP as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They were -- can you recollect where they were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- well, possibly from Nis because -- well, maybe most of them were from Nis and it was a combined detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember the number under which they -- or by which they were known?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could turn over to page 10 of the English, still on the same page for you, I know you were not at this meeting on the 7th but your SUP chief was and I wonder if he told you about this. Ilic said: "A meeting was held with VJ top officials at which it was agreed that measures were being applied but they weren't sufficient ..." Did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is that, but I do not seem to remember that kind of a comment made by my chief at that meeting, if I've been clear on this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plan of enhanced activity, including restoring the territory, that is how I would put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can go to the very last point General Ilic made it says: "In cases of restoring terrain, any information about an event must be corroborated by correct data and a case file with all the attachments must be set up."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the person who was taking the minutes just tried to shorten things, abbreviate them. We're going back to the basis of police action now. I think that this sentence of the generals must have been a lot longer. I don't know why it is so short here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know a man named Gvozden Gagic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand he worked for the OKP in Belgrade or in MUP headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't really matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Still on page 10 of the English, and if you could go to the next page in B/C/S, it's General Lukic talking. He makes reference to: "The number of 27 crimes of murder is not realistic." And then if you go to the second bullet point of that he says: "You must not wait in cases of arson and murder; the suspects must be handed over together with a criminal report to the competent judge at once. And you must ask for a sentence to be pronounced immediately." He says: "These sorts of problems have still not been cleared up ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: discussion or those remarks of General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were always encouraged and that is what our chief of SUP said and this came from the meetings too. There were uncovered crimes and we wanted -- we were supposed to contribute to a maximum to having these crimes uncovered. We were always asked to work more efficiently. It was nothing strange to me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask that all other microphones be switched off, we can barely hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were always encouraged to lay

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: territory with that kind of population are ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you finish your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I sort of thought that I should tell you how big the territory is and what kind of things happened in that territory, before the war too in peacetime we tried to uncover as many crimes as we could and we did this in all sincerity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Gagic testified about this when he was here, and at page 24523, line -- beginning at line 17 he told us that it was actually signed by General Ilic in the original and that he, Gagic, had helped draft the plan and that General Lukic -- that they had not asked the permission or informed General Lukic that they were sending this out under his name. Do you have any reason to disagree with any of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what Gagic said, I think he said the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who is --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, I assume. Perhaps there's other people around with that nickname, it doesn't really have to be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In e-court I have two versions of the B/C/S. I don't know if we can go to the next page in e-court. There's one that has that handwritten nickname you mentioned, and -- okay, that's the second page of that document. I think -- if we could go to the next page I think there's another copy. Now, you see that on the screen now? I have another copy of this same document, the type font seems to be different and it doesn't have any handwritten nickname on it. Do you know where this copy came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot help you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I will tell you the last page of this document also has the title and the handwritten name of General Lukic on it. But do you know where a copy of the original with General Ilic's signature might be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen it, I cannot help you with that. It probably stayed somewhere back there in our records that were not moved. When I say "down there," I'm referring to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have to be checked as well. I think the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there is something I'd like to add to that. I acted on the basis of that document -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's all right. Would it be standard practice for a document to be sent out with the MUP staff header and General Lukic's name on it without General Lukic being asked permission or informed that it had gone out, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that I have to object here first. It should be established first how many documents from the MUP staff the gentleman received to -- otherwise he wouldn't know what's common practice in MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm content to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right. You wouldn't send out an unsigned document with his typewritten name on it without either having his permission or without telling him afterward that you had done so, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably I wouldn't do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, do you recall if you ever did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? There were two questions, I think. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you said most probably you never would do that. I'm asking you if you remember ever having done such a thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean send a document without a signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sending a document with your SUP chief's typewritten name on it without signing it and/or without informing him afterward that you had done that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I would have acted in that way, but I could have

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about an answer you gave concerning this document. You were asked why Ilic might have sent it this way. You said another thing -- this is at page 54 yesterday, line 4. You said: "Another thing is possible too, that there's an obligation that crops up for us vis-a-vis the staff to send reports." What did you mean by that? You had an obligation under this document to send reports to the MUP staff, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our documents you can see that we informed the staff and the MUP in a parallel fashion, that's perhaps what I had in mind. According to the instructions it was our obligation to inform our administrations, and that was quite precise and the operations centre, and we were also to convey information to the staff, but this was for purposes of information only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said. There's nothing I could add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. We can see in the next-to-the-last paragraph that one of the things that you are supposed to do is immediately inform the MUP and the crime police administration of the results of the undertaken activities, and above that the paragraph says: "The coordination shall be undertaken by the MUP staff and the crime police administration." Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coordination shall be undertaken by the MUP staff and the crime police administration, yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to your statement, Exhibit 6D1631. I

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to define the word defectology, I couldn't add anything, but it's not related to our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if it's not related to your work, can you give me just a rough description of what it's about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with certain problems, problems that children, people, and others might have, that's what the term defectology means. But this education was outside the framework of my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. It sounds like it's something to do with the study of antisocial behaviour of human beings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 2 you told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I -- we've had already a description of this. Does the subject cover both -- does it also cover personal disabilities, either physical or mental?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At paragraph 2 you tell us about your various jobs you've held.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you still work there now, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what my document stated -- that's my current appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 7, the next-to-the-last sentence you say: "Naturally every member of the army and police was duty-bound to report criminal acts for which they had knowledge." Where does that duty come from? Is it a law? Is it a constitutional provision? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know to whom they're duty-bound to report? Is it to the police? To a prosecutor? To a judge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that they can report everyone on an independent basis, they can select one of the three individuals that you have referred to. There was not just one person they had to report to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 8 you talk about the border belt or the border area. You say: "Civilian investigating judges didn't go out for on-site investigations in that territory because they didn't have jurisdiction." But if a civilian committed a crime against another civilian within that 10-kilometre border area, would that case eventually come to civilian authorities for court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I say this I have war in mind, I have -- I'm thinking of war time-periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a different regime in force in that belt then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have understood each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's my understanding of the evidence we've had so far, Mr. Hannis. Is it yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure it is either, but if that's his understanding I'll move to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's look at peacetime, though. Are you saying that after the border belt had been extended but before the war began, if a civilian committed a crime against another civilian that that would be the subject of military proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You go on in that paragraph to say that during the war you didn't perform on-site investigations in those areas. I can understand that. But you said: "Nor did the police have any activities in these zones." Aren't you aware that there were numerous joint MUP and VJ actions within that border belt area during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Is your belief that the police only operated in the interior of Kosovo and didn't take part in any actions within the border belt during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know -- well, I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 9 you talk about: "With regard to the crime of terrorism OKP operatives could carry out investigations, arrest the perpetrators." But you say: "The police questioning for suspects for terrorism was undertaken in cooperation with the RDB."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were the interviews conducted jointly or did the RDB do the interviews by themselves or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, they worked independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that the case during the war or before the war or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case both before the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What about the PJP - because there's some confusion in my mind about whether they're an organizational unit or not - were they required to inform you if they knew about events constituting crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not an organizational unit. As for their duty to inform, well it wasn't a regular duty -- this paragraph refers to the work of organizational units within the SUP, those units that were involved in crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that in this paragraph you don't see that such an obligation existed, but naturally it was their

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: there's nothing more I could say about that. Now, you would have to put

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I understand about that general obligation you told us about earlier in your statement in paragraph 7, but this particular obligation did it apply to the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The instructions on crime prevention in SUP are specific, and it refers to organizational units, it refers to work at the level of the SUP. So those are the organizational units referred to, the units that are part of the SUP, the secretariat of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Move to paragraph 20, please, and you mention that -- you talk about the system reporting and that you reported to the SUP chief at

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have the war in mind or that period in mind, it was not that frequently; but in peacetime it was done regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regularly is daily or three times a week? What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a confusion. The witness said "every day" in peacetime and it was translated this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that right, Witness, every day during peacetime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime, yes; but in wartime, a little less frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall PJP commanders in your area attending collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 27 you talk about the process that takes place when a crime is reported or information about a crime is obtained. You said: "The first task is to check the information and record it in the events log." Is the events log some kind of register or book that was kept in every police station or every SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Events log is a log in which you note all the incidents. It's kept in the SUP duty section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if a crime were first reported to an OUP, did they have an events log or did they forward the information to the SUP to be recorded in the events log kept there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they have their own events log and they keep such a log for their own area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mention the second task is to inform the duty judge, and the third task is to form an on-site team, the fourth task to receive a report and take action according to the instruction and record the report in the events log. I'm unclear about a criminal complaint and a criminal report. Can you explain the difference between those two things for me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are we dealing with now? A criminal report -- did I use that term somewhere or is this something you are asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I saw it in one of the other paragraphs because the Judge asked you a question about it, and it talked about -- I think paragraph 32. The English translation I had said: "The criminal report is filed for almost every crime and only exceptionally is a report drafted." I think you explained to Judge Bonomy when he asked you a question about that that it should be a criminal complaint is filed for almost every crime with the relevant prosecutor and only exceptionally is a report drafted. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you said criminal report, that was what was in question. We have clarified this now. Would you like me to provide you with additional clarification? When the perpetrator is unidentified, then you file a criminal report. That's an example I've provided you with, that in the meantime if there's additional information, if light is shed on the case, if the perpetrator is found, then you write a special report or report that is drafted as an addition to the criminal report. And in certain cases, times of war, reports would be drafted on the NATO air-strikes because one was not in a position to describe adequately those incidents, but nevertheless they were a form of crime. That's what I can remember, and this was in agreement with the prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you look for a moment at paragraph 29, I think maybe there's a translation question there. It says: "After the on-site investigation was finished, if MUP officers had conducted the on-site investigation without the presence of an investigative judge in accordance with his authorisation, they would compile a record and a criminal report, and if the criminal report was not filed a report was drafted." That -- that's confusing to me. It seems like there are two different kinds of reports and I'm not sure what the difference is between a record and a criminal report. Can you clarify for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Three words, we have three words "zapisnik," meaning record, criminal report, "krivicno prijeva," and then we have report, "izvestaj," so I don't know how to solve this in translation but we have three terms, not two, and in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are they the three separate things referred to in the second sentence and indeed the end of the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we shall note that and interpret the English in light of what you say. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that reports on crimes committed were recorded in criminal records or the crime register and the special register kept at the level of the SUP. Can you explain to me the difference between the KU, crime register, and the PU, special register? What's the difference between those two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special register would be used to file such reports, like the reports on the NATO bombing. They would also file reports on less-serious crimes that were the result of private complaints, whereas all other forms of crime would be entered in KU, they have more or less the same weight. So don't be confused. It's just a manner of organizing these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'll do my best. You mention in paragraph 35 that during the work on crimes of order the presence is mandatory for a physician who pronounces death. Does that include at exhumations as well, is it required for a physician to be present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exhumations are performed when this is ordered by the judge. He provides for all measures, and there's no margin for manoeuvre. The judge decides on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll come back to that later. I have a question regarding something in 6D614, but let me continue through your statement for a moment. You say in paragraph 36 that the police did not perform

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: trained to sanitization of the terrain because this was a strictly military function. But then in paragraph 37 you say: "We would go out to the site of a discovery of a corpse and the corpse would be transferred to relatives or we would bury them ourselves." I guess I'm thinking of sanitization of the terrain includes removing corpses from the area, and that is something that you in the police did sometimes, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "remove" -- well, in what sense are you using that term?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Physically picking up the body where it's found and taking it away somewhere and burying it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The investigating judge performed such acts, and we sometimes did this on behalf of the judge but the judge decided about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand the judge made the decision, but the physical act, as I understand from paragraph 37, was done by you in the MUP with the assistance of civilian protection, a civilian safety and public hygiene company is how it is in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the JKP was included in the action, but the judge also had to decide. The JKP charged for this work. I didn't have any funds from which I could pay them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Paragraph 40 you provide us some statistics

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 13 June 1999, 540 general crimes were registered, which includes murder, bodily harm, terrorism, and theft."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: non-Albanian citizens and 346 against Albanian victims." 351 plus 346 is 697, compared to the 540 you mention in paragraph 40. Can you explain the difference? Is the difference that this is for all of 1999, including after you left in mid-June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You found that where?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, the years are different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the periods are certainly different, but you say the years are different?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think in paragraph 40 it says during 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And 70 [sic] it says 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I was reading from the third line in the course of 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's 1999 in the third line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you find those two paragraphs, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have obviously made a -- an accurate conclusion. Since there was this increase that means that the figures after our withdrawal were included as well, that mostly related to certain crimes involving kidnapping and so on, abduction and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mean the -- let's see, 697 minus 540 equals 157. Do you mean there were 157 additional crimes that occurred after June 13th, 1999, that are in paragraph 75?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that it's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But it sounds like you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should be. I hope I'm being clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where would that information have come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our information about the abductions came from the families of victims or through other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go to paragraph 45. You say: "The KLA introduced attacks that it used to finance itself." How did you know about that, what was your source of information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 3 per cent. That was the tax that everybody had to pay, everybody who had companies, and that was a tax --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop, please. My question is: How did you know about that? What was your source of information that that existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some receipts and also from talking to some Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And further on in that paragraph you mention that: "The Albanians had to hand-over any weapons and ammunition they legally owned which they received, as did everyone else legally from the SUP, to the KLA." My first question is: Are you talking about arms that had been furnished to the Kosovo Albanians by the SUP or by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they had a permit to possess and carry a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're aware, aren't you, that in 1998 as part of the joint summer anti-terrorist action conducted by the MUP and VJ that numerous Siptar or Kosovo Albanian villages were disarmed, their weapons were handed in or taken in? You knew about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In Exhibit P2166, which is a record of a meeting of the operations inter-departmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo, we've seen a report that some 93 Siptar Albanian villages were disarmed during that operation or that action and 38 of those were in

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: that were disarmed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is a different kind of fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in -- while I was speaking of that document, in paragraph 101 you talk about: "In 1998 and 1999 the PJP brought in large groups of people collected from the zones of combat operations." Now say that approximately 1421 persons were detained initially and most of them were released, 337 persons were arrested. Is that for the entire time-period throughout the war as well as in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1998 and during wartime. You can see it above as well. These are the people who had been brought in because they were believed to have participated in terrorist actions as members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: the entirety of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You talk about some of the incidents listed in the indictment that were shown to you. On a number of them you indicated you had no

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crime police as police functions on the basis of a report given by citizens. At that point in time we were in a grave problem. The Albanians fearing the KLA did not even report some of the incidents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: field and they did not establish these -- this either, despite the problems that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't see any police or VJ going from house to

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you with full responsibility that there was no such

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: was full of inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: municipality, if not that the town itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: you have no information about that. We've seen a document in this case, Exhibit P2002, an afteraction report of a joint VJ/MUP operation that

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30.000 refugees were assisted. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive these reports, so if you're trying to say that I was supposed to know about this on the basis of these reports I'm telling you that I did not receive these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. No, I'm just asking --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nor could I know this through some other sources, as I've told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know the figure. I know that there was some, but I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. There was one company part of

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we'll confine ourselves to evidence from the witness at the moment, Mr. Lukic. You can coordinate all the evidence at a later stage. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 64 you talk about the indictment paragraph 75(d) which talks about the killing of members of the Berisha family in Suva Reka. And you say you didn't know about it at the time but you learned about it later. You're aware that Colonel Radoslav Mitrovic has been charged, I understand, and is being prosecuted in Belgrade in connection with that event; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one reason you didn't know about the number that had died was because a few dozen of them had been hauled off in a truck shortly after the killings, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult to carry out an on-site investigation in Suva Reka because the town, half of it was under the control of the KLA, so that was an additional factor. What you're saying is something I have learned of later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 58 of your statement concerning the allegations about deportations from Suva Reka, you say that: "The incidents in Suva Reka as described do not stand and are not true, almost the entire city, not half as you just said, almost the entire city of Suva Reka was in the hands of the KLA." How do you account for Colonel Mitrovic and forces with him managing to go in and kill some 44 members of the Berisha family under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is still my position that the KLA had under its control the larger part of the town and constantly carried out provocations. We conditionally speaking had part of the road under our control, the OUP building, and some Albanians. When you're saying how come they were able to enter, my explanation is that the KLA didn't really worry about everything. They had the town under their control for a very practical reason, so that they could be able to attack police and the police building. Now, as to how they came in, I don't know, I have no information to that effect. The trial is still in progress and we will see what they will establish. If he's found to be guilty, he will be sentenced, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 68 you talk about seeing the statement of Rashit Salihi and the incident in Celina village on 25 March 1999. You comment on the fact that he mentions police in black uniforms and you say no one in the police wore black uniforms. Do you know if anybody in the JSO ever wore black uniforms during 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999 nobody wore black uniforms. As far as I know, black uniforms are worn by the SAJ members and they wear it for anti-terrorist actions in urban environment and at night, and back in 1999 I never saw anybody wear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about anybody in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm looking at one of the incidents reported in Exhibit 6D614, and I'm not sure how to get to the page number. It's page number 19 of the translation I was working on when I found this item, which is under 56.1.2, offences involving identified perpetrators and measures taken against VJ personnel. The 6D page number I have is 6D19-0134 for the English, it's event number 18, but I don't know what the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All pages are the same in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could try then page 19. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Item number 18 in Donje Nerodimlje in Urosevac municipality, the 28th of April, 1999, it talks about some individuals in military uniforms, most probably volunteers. But if you'll go down it talks about four individuals -- and this is in the second paragraph, halfway through, four individuals in VJ uniforms burst into the premises of the department, the MUP, they started to shout and threaten if the girls weren't handed back to them, one of them who was wearing a black uniform. So this is in one of your reports in 6D614 that's making reference to apparently some VJ personnel wearing a black uniform. You were not aware of that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is not something that happened in my territory, and from what I can see this came on the basis of a statement given by the injured party. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the first line says: "Marinkovic Jovanka ... phoned to the police ..."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that "the police --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That a patrol came, and after talking to them we learned that, and then the text follows about everything that they heard after they talked to the injured party. So that means that this information came from them, that's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness, I think, has made that clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that at the very outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, and I don't dispute that, I do too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, at -- I'm referring to an internal OTP document of a report about that mission, and I just want to ask you some questions about what Mr. Michael Hehn, a member of the leadership research team in the OTP said and asked if you remember this or agree or disagree with it. He

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would need to give me more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's 2006.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at paragraph 105 of your statement, please, and could you read that out aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's very different than the English translation I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This again raises the issue I have about who translated which portions of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that's -- Mr. Lukic, I appreciate that there are times when a little word-for-word translation is not possible, but that translation is inadequate, it omits a substantial part of what is contained in the B/C/S paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I don't think so that we did this paragraph, I'll check.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that paragraph 106 describes it further in even greater detail more specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not only that, but the last sentence in English doesn't apparently exist in the B/C/S text either. We'll come back to that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One must bear in mind paragraph 106 as well and then that is correct wording. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please now read paragraph 106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That again is rather different from the existing which is -- which contains the date March 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you also read, please, paragraph 107.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 147 you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 107, the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "After receiving the task that" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is reading 108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 107, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the last three lines of the English version do not appear in the B/C/S version. Mr. Hannis, did you get from CLSS a note of the paragraphs that were translated by them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Your Honour. I only got that they had done 90 paragraphs, and we have 122, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall try to get that information because I think what is necessary here is to separate the two and decide whether we are prepared to admit the parts that were not translated by CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Meanwhile we can continue with your cross-examination, Mr. Hannis. If any other difficulty of this kind emerges, then we'll just have to go through this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, I'll continue on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never even came to see me in terms of my work and he never exerted any influence over the plan documents that I created. When I say "plan documents," those are the documents that envisage further work on that, that I had created then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it seems that he did have some input over how this was organized and what kind of documents you were collecting, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that he supported in a way what I suggested, approved of it, supported it, let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I take it you went to him to get his approval because you weren't going to go forward without it, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use the word approval here specifically, in a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there was no need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's time for our break, Your Honour. I'm not quite finished yet, I may have another half-hour, if permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it is a very detailed statement and there are complications caused by the translation. I think you should regard that as an outside limit, though, Mr. Hannis. We have to have a break at this stage, sir. Could you please again leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it has emerged during the break that not only are there paragraphs translated by your team added to the version which was translated by CLSS, but there are alterations also to the paragraphs -- some of the paragraphs that were translated by CLSS. So this is a more major exercise than it looked. Now, once a mind is applied to it, it may not turn out to be all that difficult to sort it out. But we shall have to revise the status of the Exhibit 6D1631 to that of marked for identification until we are satisfied that an accurate translation of what has been signed in B/C/S has been produced. Now, it would be unreasonable to require CLSS to revise the whole of the document; however, every additional paragraph that was prepared and translated by your team must be submitted by you to them for revisal of your translations. And secondly, you must identify every passage in the original CLSS translated version that you have interfered with since you got their translation so that they can revise that also. But -- now, that's the bit that may prove a bit tricky. You will have to go through it in a painstaking fashion to do that for the reason I've just given, that it would be unreasonable use of our resources, limited resources, to require them to revise the whole of that document. Now, do you understand all of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we intend to do so, but we really didn't have time yesterday and we ask for your patience and to give us at least the dead-line after the -- this weekend so we can revise it during the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, are you content that we fix the dead-line, let's say Wednesday of next week, a week for today, from that exercise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, but I have a request that depending on how that comes out that I have the option perhaps to re-call this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- to ask about something. That can be done by videolink for his convenience, but you understand my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've been very fortunate that generally speaking -- in fact, I think in all instances when this has -- this sort of situation has arisen or you've expressed a reservation about the possibility of re-calling a witness that it has not turned out to be necessary. But we recognise that that always remains a possibility. I think just on reflection, Mr. Lukic, since we finish next Thursday for the break we'll say close of business on Tuesday, so 5.00 on Tuesday is the -- 4.00, in fact, on Tuesday is the dead-line for you to file the revised translation, always assuming that CLSS can accommodate you but we will ask them very nicely to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue now, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a related concern on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If this has happened with any other witness statements, then I have a concern that witnesses who have come in and identified the statement in the Serbian language as their own and what we're relying on in the English may be something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be a weakness in the Rules that no form of certification is required for translations of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but my particular problem with this one related to the fact that with the header on it, I assumed it was a CLSS translation and that was misleading and I don't know if that's happened on any others, but that was the crux of my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regarding this misleading issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the question is: Are there others where because you have been dealing with these at the wire you have actually -- and I use the word not pejoratively - where you've interfered with the CLSS translation and yet it might appear on the document that it was a translation done in its entirety by CLSS?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know about this case, and we really did interfere with some paragraphs completely, we added some paragraphs and we did add some additions. And as you saw here in 107 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has that happened in relation to other witnesses is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to check it because we had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that by Tuesday of next week you should clarify that to Mr. Hannis because he has, as I understand it, at least some resources available to him to check these things if they are identified to him. So I think you owe it to him to point out any similar examples so that he can double-check. All right. So please do that by Tuesday also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in relation to this latter point, that's whether any other documents have - and I assume that's confined to statements - have received similar treatment, we require a filing from you by next Tuesday on that topic to clarify the position for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Hannis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to check, I'm not sure in terms of anything I could say now, but that would be my answer at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm still not clear. What did the minister tell you in terms of you having overstepped your authority? Did he make reference to something specific or did you know what he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you put each of these and turn on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then put the other one on the ELMO, please. What is that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document -- could you scroll down, please, so that I can see the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go on, line 13 says my family has suffered I don't want them to suffer anymore, I believe the witness said my family lives from my salary. I think that part came through -- if we can have that part checked, it's on page 54, line 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes sense. We did hear reference to something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness, it's important when you're answering questions to speak as clearly as you can into these microphones, otherwise it may be difficult for the interpreter to hear exactly what

utterances.text: Thank you.
