utterances.text: Thank you. The last paragraph in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's a good idea. Does this log-book still exist today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where we might look for a copy of it or who we should ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, my last topic I wanted to ask you about is this Exhibit 6D614, and it's in paragraph 114 in your statement. You talk about how this comprehends digest of security events which represents committed crime and activities of the police. So this 700-page some document, these are not all of the crimes that you have records of from 1998 and 1999; is that right? These are just selected ones that were collected for purposes of putting together this overview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only limitation is the time-period. All registered incidents which represent a crime were registered for a certain period of time, for a given period of time, and that's what this document contains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This purports to cover the time-period from 1 July 1998 to 20 June 1999; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: identified perpetrators and measures taken against police officers. And there are 33 separate items under that section. So does that mean that there were a total of 33 cases between July 1998 and June 1999 in which there were recorded criminal offences where the perpetrators were identified as being police officers? And that's the grand total, that's all of them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that doesn't mean that that's the grand total. That could mean that that's the smallest number that was available based on the information available at the time when this document was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm trying to figure out. Is this all-inclusive, or is this something that's supposed to be a representative sample and here are some samples where police were perpetrators and here's some samples where VJ were perpetrators and here's some samples where KLA were perpetrators. It's something less than the total of all recorded crimes in Kosovo, right, it's a selection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we've had some information about the number of police officers that were prosecuted during that time-period, which seems to be a much higher number than the 33 that we have in this exhibit -- well, and I'll grant you it's 33 separate incidents, but the total number of individual perpetrators is not a whole lot higher than 33. Can you explain that difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I summarized an event where there were two or more perpetrators and that that's how you arrive at the situation where you have more perpetrators than events. But I am not certain until I look at the document because I know that there were no limitations, and I included everything that was provided to me, I summarized everything.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: that crime police documents are of such nature that one cannot tamper with them, write something that's -- shouldn't be there. All of these documents were produced at the time when these events took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I suggest to you that police documents are really no better or no worse when it comes to a question of being tampered with; it depends on the people involved, doesn't it? Any document can be tampered with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to a crime report, say, that was written on the 1st of April, 1999, and sent to various addressees, that cannot be amended afterwards. And when I said this, these are the kinds of documents that I had in mind. This crime report was put into a system, it's a uniform information system, and I don't think that somebody can put in any amendments, changes. Perhaps it is possible, I don't know, I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about just a couple of entries in this and then I'll finish. At page 8, it's item number 14, if we can see that in e-court. This is in the section involving offences with identified perpetrators and measures taken against police officers. This is about an incident in Podujevo on the 28th of March, 1999, in which a group of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've found there are a number of sections, and this page 8 seems to deal with -- oh, it's an incident in Klina. Is that what you're looking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, at the bottom item number 18 should be Podujevo and then it carries on to page number 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see that one, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know when this particular one was written, this summary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to say. I would need to check that. I would have to look at the file and there is a date there at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see that this report indicates that on the 30th of March, two days after the event, members of the public informed the department of interior that there were several bodies in houses and on business premises at a particular location. Going over to the next page of the English, page 9, members of the SAJ reserve police force, and it names a couple, used fire-arms against a group of civilians and they killed some named individuals. The incident occurred on the 28th of March. 15 people, women and children, were not identified. Now, we've had evidence in this court from, first of all, Goran Stoparic, who was a member of that SAJ reserve group in Podujevo, and he tells us about what happened that day. And we had more recently Colonel Zivaljevic, Dragan Zivaljevic, who was a commander of a PJP brigade. And in his statement, which is Exhibit 6D1606 at paragraph 37 he talks about this event and he says: "Immediately upon finding out about the incident, I went to the chief of the Podujevo OUP since I found myself then not far from the building to confirm this information. During the course of our conversation with the chief Zoran Simovic, the assistant SAJ commander came in and he partially explained the details, and it was agreed that all the necessary steps would be taken," et cetera. He also noted that some policemen from the 22nd PJP Detachment had actually provided first aid and assistance to the injured victims at the site and carried injured children to the doctors. So are you telling me this happened, all those other police knew about it, and no one reported it to the MUP or to the OUP in Podujevo until two days later and those were members of the public? That doesn't make sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain this to you. Would you please put the copy back on, page 2, where it says that the investigating judge from Prokoplje conducted an on-site investigation. Perhaps you failed to notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I did notice that. My question is: Why is it something that was well-known to lots of police in the town, reportedly not noticed or not officially registered until two days after the event, when supposedly members of the public informed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply wanted to assist you. There's nothing strange about that. Crime policemen from the Pristina SUP wrote that report. You didn't put the document back for me. I will try to explain to you. It is most likely that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please put it back on the screen. It's page 8 and 9, number 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the English page. I think the B/C/S page may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we were told is the pages were identical in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's correct. Yeah, it starts on the bottom of this page, but I think the witness may need the next page for the part he wanted to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here that the on-site investigation was conducted by the investigating judge from Prokoplje. So it's possible that the crime policemen from the Pristina SUP who summarized this did not have sufficient information on the first day about operatives in Podujevo having done all that and that the misunderstanding stems from that. There was no ill intention in it. Since this is a unique case, because the district court from Pristina should have had jurisdiction because Podujevo falls under the Pristina district court. But instead of that it seems that it was the investigative judge from Prokoplje who was competent to act in that case, but there was no ill intention. I think that everything that you stated does exist in the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you another possible explanation for why there's no indication of a report until two days later is because Mr. Stoparic told us after this event occurred all the SAJ reservists were rounded up, severely chastised, put on a bus, and returned to Serbia. And I suggest to you that there was a delay in reporting about this because the police were hoping to cover it up and keep it quiet, and only until some citizens came in and reported it did it get noted down even though the OUP chief and lots of other police in town were well aware that the event had transpired. Isn't that a possible explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have information concerning that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done the crime policemen of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see this is apparently some information received from Captain Krsmanovic and Major Corbic from the VJ. Several dozen bodies, between 30 and 40, were lying near the village cemetery in this village of Rezalo, they had been covered by earth and rubble by members of the army. At the bottom of the next paragraph, you'll see the investigating magistrate refused to issue exhumation orders since damage may have been caused to the bodies. And then the next paragraph, another judge, apparently investigating magistrate, authorised officers went to the scene, established that there were a large number of bodies underneath the earth but that investigating magistrate refused to issue orders for exhumation and instead issued orders that one more layer - and you have to go to the next page in English - one more layer of approximately 80 cubic metres [sic] of earth be deposited over it. And at that time he insisted with the army officers that they should carry out the investigation and there's no further information about it. Do you know anything more about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know more than what you said to me. We would need to look into the file and see if there's anything else there. Although I personally think that the army was involved and they took over, I guess. That's what I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that takes me to, I guess, my last question. I didn't see on any of these involving identified perpetrators what the outcome of proceedings were. Sometimes there's an indication of criminal complaint was filed or something was sent to the Prosecutor's office. But you don't have any information about the outcome of any of these cases, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these cases were summarized on the basis of documentation which was compiled during the war, at that time. It is the courts that

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: authority would he be assigned there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that a term was used here by the Defence attorney and I don't know if I used that, but he had the work obligation to do that, whether that is wartime assignment, I'm not a soldier, I really cannot interpret that, but it was his work obligation so he was under that director.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does that relieve him of serving in the military during wartime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would look now, please, at paragraph 75 and then you have 76 until 80. Now, in these paragraphs you give a large number of statistics. What is the source of all these statistics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used tables that I have here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who compiled the tables?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are these records any part of the case evidence so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we didn't have time to translate them and to submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But if you want to get it from the witness, I think that he was willing to provide it for Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Thank you. If you could go now, please, to paragraph 110, and you were asked

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they would help, certainly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question. If I have a look at what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said to us that as regards some information on PJP actions you found that in the surveys of the MUP staff for Kosovo. In these surveys, did you find information about actions of the PJP or about security-related incidents that were reported on from these actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter. Perhaps I didn't specify it right. In the daily reports I did not confine myself to the survey, so the security-related incident was like the one in Bela Crkva that was -- that meant that after an anti-terrorist action a corpse had been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the example that I had given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I'm not clear, Mr. Lukic, what documents we are referring to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we can have P1693 on the screen because Mr. Hannis used this one, P16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The surveys to which you refer are --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we heard that the translation of bulletin, it's the document composed by the MUP staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is to report to Belgrade you mean, is it? Or it's to report to the SUPs in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the document composed by the MUP staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but sent where? Here we see that it's sent to the ministry in Belgrade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: document was sent to the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, it is the 1st of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time were communications disrupted in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for information in Kosovo, on the 1st of May, 1999, how did information get through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very slowly and with a several-day delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see these surveys or overviews?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where they were sent to the SUPs in KiM?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in which period they were sent to the SUPs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in quite a few cases. I can say there are some from 1998 and some in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever come across in such documents reports that refer to the course of PJP actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what you're getting at. When I said "reports," I did not mean combat reports and there's no way they could be here. I meant security-related incidents that were the possible result of these anti-terrorist actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are rather voluminous documents, voluminous reports. You really had to ask me specifically about combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Hannis asked you and now I am trying to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. Whoever it was that had asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Going back just slightly to what you said, you referred a moment ago to combat reports. What do you mean by these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anti-terrorist actions, that's what I meant. I may have made a mistake in terms of military terminology, please appreciate that I'm not a soldier, that cannot be contained in these surveys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But are you saying that the PJP wrote combat reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I assume, I assume, that they are -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, it was your words, Witness. You say: "You really had to ask me specifically about combat reports." Can you clarify what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I the one who's supposed to explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They're your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody misunderstood what I said, that the survey contained PJP reports on anti-terrorist actions. I was misunderstood. I said that had someone explained to me that it was those actions that were concerned, I used the term "combat reports." I meant that these reports could not have been incorporated in this type of survey. That is why there was this error when I said that they could be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm certainly not following you. You were asked a question: "Did you ever come across such documents, reports, that refer to the course of PJP actions?" And you then said: "I see what you're getting at. When I said 'reports,' I did not mean combat reports and there's no way they could be here." Now, what were you referring to by "combat reports"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reports on anti-actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But after referring to combat reports and saying there's no way they could be here you then said: "I meant security-related incidents that were the possible result of these anti-terrorist actions." So there's a distinction being made between reports of security-related incidents and combat reports, and I'm anxious to understand the distinction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anti-terrorist actions and reports on them are something that I never had, but I did have cases when I registered cases when a security-related incident is linked up to an anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that doesn't tell me what you mean by "combat reports."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anti-terrorist without any previous military knowledge, perhaps that was a mis-characterization, anti-terrorist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since yesterday have you had communication with anybody about this case and about any of the evidence in the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, every time you use a name you cause me to redact a part of the transcript. So could you do your best, please, to avoid the use of the name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know, first of all, whether the PJP wrote combat reports at all or reports on anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I did not see that so I do not know about that. They may have written something like that it seems, but I cannot testify about any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did the PJP members report to first of all on security-related incidents, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that they sent reports to their superior, or rather, if they are in action then the person who was in charge of that action; that would seem logical to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know in territorial terms who they reported to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it concerns a crime, then there is local jurisdiction straight away of the SUP; and later on, the court comes into the picture as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the SUPs reported to about security-related incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They reported the MUP and the judiciary organs in terms of the type involved, that is to say if it was a crime, and other organs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they report to anyone in Pristina about security-related incidents, the SUPs from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is the staff, and our duty was to supply information to them on an informative basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This information about security-related incidents, can that be found in these surveys of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they are contained in our information as well, they depended on us, what we submitted to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that it's time for the break now and that we will have to continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to have a break at this stage again, so could you leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you again at ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can carry on, can we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 6D666 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They had the obligation with regard to these documents that were drafted in the course of the war, with regard to these documents that concerned security incidents, they had the obligation to process these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many days they spent there, how many people were involved on those two or three occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the last occasion quite clearly. There were about four or five individuals, there was a lady among them, I remember that, and they spent several days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're a peaceful and calm man, that's not characteristic in the Balkans. I think this is the impression that the Chamber has gained too and you don't want to make any very strong statements, but let me put the following question to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about 6D874.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And while waiting for the document to appear on the screen so as not to waste any more time, this is a document sent from the staff drafted by General Ilic, Dragan Ilic. We just need this document as a basis for my question. Have a look at the document. Is that the one I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Dragan Ilic act in accordance with Sreten Lukic's authorisation or someone else's authorisation or did he not require any authorisation? How did he proceed, can you explain this for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that he didn't need Sreten Lukic's authorisation. He performed his duties, and I'd be inclined to say that this was within his remit and that he was only doing his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We were also trying to establish when you draft a criminal report or criminal complaint and when you draft a report, so I'll put the following question to you. If we're dealing with murder [as interpreted] what sort of a report is drafted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in such a case, and you're quite right, you only draft a report. This didn't occur to me, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: If it's a matter of suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, it says "murder" and the word was "suicide." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 26, line 20, you were asked about weapons that had been seized, that had to do with a paragraph in your statement, paragraph 45.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was a different kind of weapon, that's what you said, and my question is as follows. What weapon -- what kind of weapon was seized, what category did that weapon belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapon seized didn't fall into the category of weapons that can be legally possessed. We were dealing with automatic rifles, weapons that are used by troops. These weapons were seized, not the weapons that the Albanians possessed with permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was illegally possessed, if that's of any assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With regard to that matter I have another question for you. As far as possessing automatic weapons are concerned or any other weapons without a permit, is such possession illegal, is that a crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also shown 6D614, page 9, so could we please have this on the screen. This is a page from 6D614. I apologise, we need to see page 5. My colleague Hannis asked you a question and said that 33 criminal reports had been filed against policemen. What sort of crimes are we dealing with in this part of the document, document 6D614?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crimes concerned are very serious ones. It would be easiest for me to say that these crimes could also include murder. These crimes are complex ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does it mean, against life and limb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means that such crimes also include attacks on life and limb of the victim, so the crime is directed at the life and limb of the victim in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the various items we have here -- well, could there have been several perpetrators of the crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think it is stated somewhere here too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have page 129 of this document on the screen now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please read the title of this section.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says: "Recorded criminal offences against property involving identified perpetrators police officers."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we now have a look at page 130, the next page. Have a look at item 7.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it's about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with the crime of the abuse of office perpetrated by policemen, they are officials and given that they are officials they committed such a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What sort of policemen are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just read through this. A policeman of the Pec SUP, one is an active-duty policeman, one is a reserve policeman, and they are in Pec SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was done? What were the consequences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojkovic had his employment terminated and he was handed over to the prosecution. Radovic was also removed from the reserve forces and handed over to the district public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that there could have been several perpetrators involved in each item. Let's have a look at page 149 -- I apologise, 148. This is the last item, 99, from this group of crimes, crimes against property that is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In both cases this involves, or rather, does it involve crimes against identified or non-identified perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're looking at item 99, in this case it is the identified one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about crimes against life and limb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were against identified perpetrators as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to your statistics at the time, were there a lot of crimes committed by unidentified perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was registered by the crime police and included in my statement, the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it in the entire file?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and those were verified allegations based on which we wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you have those documents and you have them in your possession?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a topic now and I don't know how we're going to deal with it. Yesterday you gave us your position and it has to do with the use of the word - and could this be translated into English - using the term Siptar. I'm going to put questions to you, just a minute, please. When an Albanian, a mother, addresses her son would she call him Siptar or would she call him an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In their literature - and I read their books - and in their conversations they use that term among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. In newspapers, in official media, in Albanian do they use the word Siptar or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They use the word Siptar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that's because it's an Albanian word.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If my mother --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why would they speaking Albanian use the word "Albanac," or the Serb word for Albanian? That wouldn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand also, Your Honour. If my mother calls me Serb, why would I be offended if you call me Serb? I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but this exercise isn't going to help to determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have another one related to the same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've been through this before and we know that there are two words. Now, why would someone speaking one language use a word from the other language? Why do that unless you have a motive for doing it, and the question is: What is the motive? Is it a good one or a bad one. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that both words are part of Serbian language as well. Only in 1974 with the constitution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, now you're giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not expecting this witness to give us that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that he knows something else definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say that in communication among the Serbs, for example, if two Serbs were talking to each other and an Albanian would overhear them, if the word Siptar was used that would not be offensive. And in the communication among Albanians the word Siptar is used, the word Siptar means an eagle so it's not a pejorative or an offensive term, it has that background. And very often when you talk to an Albanian that word is not considered as something bad, but yesterday I said that in some cases when you address a Siptar with that term he would feel offended. That's what I said yesterday, and those were some cases that are an exception. I read their books and their other stuff and what you're saying is right, they use the word Siptar everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is not how I understood your evidence yesterday. I understood you yesterday to be saying that you did not expect the word Siptar in an official document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I said to you yesterday - and you can check, I remember this well - when this word is used in relation to a Siptar, he - and I shrug my shoulders - feels offended. I think that's what I said verbatim yesterday, but I didn't explain to you why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you're looking for what I think you're looking for yesterday's transcript at 25402, line 9 I asked a question about something in the Exhibit P1693, and from there on. That's the discussion I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer you gave yesterday, Witness, was -- you were asked: "Why do you say the use of the name Siptar was a mistake?" Which is how you put it, as a mistake in a -- and it was in a Telex. You said: "Because those Albanians thought it was a pejorative term to use. I had in mind their feelings rather than ours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation was not correct. I did not use the word "pejorative." I said that they feel offended in individual cases, in certain cases; that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It comes to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just clarified, and it's up to you to draw conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but you took the view that it was a mistake for that to appear in an official -- a document being used in official government circles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that document, as I put it, represents some sort of communication -- not a document because it would not be used in a document, but if it's a communication between two Serbs then that term can be used because it's not offensive, it would not offend an Albanian. Even if an Albanian were present that would not offend him, only if you addressed him that way. I think that Albanians overdid it a bit in that sense because they asked to be called Albanians for a practical reason; they wanted to show their affiliation, their -- the fact that they belonged to Albanian population in general. I think that that's the reason to -- background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's right, you would expect them to want to be called Siptars, to distinguish them from the Serbian use of the language. It was you who spontaneously raised this yesterday. You were not asked a question at the time it was raised. You said: "The word Siptars is a bit misplaced I think. It was the Albanian minority and this may have been a mistake." And you were then asked by Mr. Hannis: "A mistake by General Lukic or whoever wrote this report?" And your answer was: "I'm afraid that this report was not authorised."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Prosecutor used that term, Siptar, two or three times and I thought that he asked me about that word. Perhaps I spoke in haste, and this is why you were given the answer that I gave and perhaps I managed to clarify it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you something that I've asked you already today and is continuing to concern me. Have you had communication with anyone about the evidence in this case since yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, yesterday you, or rather, you attended a dinner with me and with our Albanian witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that I asked him the following: How should I address you, with the word Albanian or with the word Siptar? And do you remember what he said to me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told you that you should address him with Siptar, and that's exactly how I called him and that he was not offended by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the transcript it says that we went to dinner yesterday, whereas our Albanian witness left The Hague on Saturday; that is to say that we had dinner together several days before his testimony. Please can this be entered into the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll ask CLSS to revise the interpretation by reference to the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At page 11 on my screen at the moment, which --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreter corrected herself, I said "rather." That was a mistake on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't appear as an interpreter's correction, but we'll now note that that's what it was rather than the language used by Mr. Lukic. So there will be no need for a revisal. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. Those were all the questions I had for you. Thank you for coming here and testifying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, factually I had no tasks and that was a consequence of that. I have no other explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you receiving your salary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the other relates to the question of the computer. I haven't a great knowledge of technology, no doubt there are many around here with far greater. But I thought that the heart of a computer, the hard disk, was more or less indestructible. Is that not your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just like you, I don't have sufficient knowledge in that field and I conveyed what I had been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... perhaps ask the assistance of the technical centre since they've helped us try to recover several that have died in the course of this trial, hard drives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who was this information technology specialist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the name, but I know the man. That was eight years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that was all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly some daily surveys as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that completes your -- sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the one question I had about the break in service, the first topic you asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That now completes your evidence. Thank you for coming --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Regarding your question, Your Honour, I would just like to have a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is that? Further Re-examination by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: About the sources where we can find the evidence about the murders. Where is that source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the SUPs, that's where it is, and if you look at all the materials from Kosovo that were done, the reports on murders were done on manual typewriters. During the course of the war we didn't have any power and we didn't do that on computers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That does now complete your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher -- sorry, there is one thing which I almost forgot. Paragraph 57 of the statement -- Mr. Lukic, I had anticipated you would clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is Srbica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the witness said it was not Srbica, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in his area but it's not that Srbica, you are right. I asked him about the Srbica and I forgot that there were several Srbicas. And he said: I know nothing about those events in Srbica, but then it appeared that that Srbica from the indictment is in Kosovska Mitrovica. So my learned friend Cepic was right yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the first two sentences should be deleted, should they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the rest could apply to paragraphs 52 and 53, where it's -- it is explained about Orahovac area and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, so it can remain -- the first two sentences should be deleted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What are you saying about 52 and 53?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it applies to paragraphs 52 and 53, Celina and Nogavac and Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They should be deleted as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, they stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But that's in that area and those references to 57 should be applied to these two paragraphs, 52 and 53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I go back to what I said. Thank you for coming here. You're now free to leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the -- just hold on a second. In addition to the filings that have to be made in relation to the accuracy of the statement, we also require both the Prosecution and the Lukic Defence and any other of the accused with an interest to within the same time-period, that's a week from today, to make a submission about the extent to which that evidence requires to remain confidential. Yesterday it did seem that probably none of it required to remain confidential, but today's been rather a different position. But that's just a very general indication of an impression from listening to the evidence. Now, the next witness, Mr. Lukic -- sorry, we can now go to open session. Just hold on a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had an objection to raise concerning the exhibit 6D614. I have a general objection about the process and I have a more specific objection about several portions of it in that I don't think they have any relevance or probative value for us. There's a big section on non-violent crimes committed by unknown perpetrators between July 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a second. Mr. Lukic, is the whole of the relevant -- or what you consider the relevant parts of that exhibit now translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, this document is marked for identification, so what will happen is that there will be a filing from the Lukic Defence inviting us to admit the document, including the translation, and at that point you should respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our next witness is our expert, Mr. Branislav Simonovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Simonovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud that document now being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You asked me to make a few corrections in the introductory part before we move on to the actual subject matter. The introductory part of your findings, that doesn't pertain to the police but you insisted we clarified certain points.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off, we cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 4.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: I already have it open.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What it says here, the commander of the collective supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: As the head of the federal state ex officio, this should be deleted. Only the word "commander" should be there and it should replace the words that should be deleted, the ones that you referred to. Is that all right now? utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we'll go to the very heart of the matter first. You have paragraph Roman II in the Serbian version, Arabic 2 in the English. Can you see what it says here, what the tasks of the staff are?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see the tasks of the staff here, they're defined in the decision on forming the staff, its task is in accordance with that decision, it is to plan, organize, and manage the work of organizational units in the ministry; and also, it has to manage attached units to prevent terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. And in the second paragraph -- am I going too fast? In the second paragraph the staff's tasks said to be planning and organizing and uniting the work of organizational units of the ministry and Kosovo and Metohija and they have to carry out complex security-related tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it be possible for such staff tasks to be carried out in practice?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, on the basis of the analysis I carried out while studying the literature and while analysing the organization of the staff, the task or the tasks defined here couldn't be carried out in practice. It was an impossible mission to carry out such tasks, and we will discuss the reasons which it was impossible over the next few days. I don't think the staff could have planned or organized or led the work of organizational units of the ministry, and it couldn't have done that in the case of the attached units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What would implementing this decision have required?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: In order to implement the decision, in practice it would have been necessary to establish completely different relationships which are defined by the rules on the internal organization of the Ministry of the Interior. Such rules determine certain relationships, certain obligations of various organizational units within the system of the ministry from the top down. So some new body could have carried out the tasks assigned. It was necessary to change all the relationships, to have new rules, it was necessary to have the organizational relationship completely changed. The organizational relationship that existed pursuant to the rules that regulated police operations. But this wasn't done and it could not have been done at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, Professor, did you work out the solution to the conundrum, can you tell us why this was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm prepared to make the utmost effort to try and explain this to the Court, to try and explain why such a decision was formulated, a decision that couldn't be carried out, and I tried to explain the entire organizational system in existence, the one that I referred to in my report, and this system made it impossible in fact to carry out this decision, to implement the decision. Can I start at the first level of my analysis and then I'll follow any suggestions you may have, and I'll be quite happy to be guided by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I don't want to disturb the way in which Mr. Lukic intends to present this. I thought perhaps you had a simple answer to the conundrum, but if you don't perhaps it should be developed in questions by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript there's an interpretation which means rules. Can you tell us the name of the document that you referred to that should be changed?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if we are to discuss the system that required changes -- well, for the system to change one should have started with the rules book on the internal organization of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, so this is a rules book or these are rules adopted by the Ministry of the Interior, and these rules regulate the system of internal organization and of leadership within the ministry, from the top down. And the tasks assigned to the staff if they were to be carried out it would be necessary to change the entire system. Why wasn't that possible at the time? Well for two reasons. One was a formal legal reason and there was another substantial reason. May I continue? What's the formal legal reason? What should have been changed? Assigned to the staff tasks that they could carry out within the system in existence in the Ministry of the Interior. Well, it would have been necessary to issue a new rules book, and these rules would have to be adopted at governmental level. The rules is a document that determines the internal organizational systems within each ministry. One of the rules books is the book that dealt with the internal organization with the Ministry of the Interior, but to act in this way in accordance with the law in force at the time, it would have been necessary to issue a new rules book with a fairly complex procedure contained within it. And one you would have had to have in the document called the decree on the principles for the internal organization and systemization of work posts in ministries, and in special organizations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it all of this is clearly set out in the report, Mr. Lukic, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually it's not. We have to go through some points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's the report all about then? Because it's a very heavy document to read and to take in. utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, I'll try to continue that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's just I'm expressing anxiety since we have a whole catalogue of experts coming later. The whole point of this is to identify the answers to the conundrums in the report. utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked the same question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.text: By presenting the expert analysis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean there's an English saying that where there's a will there's a way; in other words, if you want to do something you can achieve it, to hell with the rules.

utterances.text: In police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer here that we're getting is: No, the rules are there and you can't do anything because the rules stop you. Well, I have a great big question mark over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in relation to the former Yugoslavia. So let's be realistic about this and try to get to answers, real, genuine answers to the questions that trouble the Trial Chamber.

utterances.text: Well, please continue.

utterances.text: If we are. utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. So there is already concern, I can tell you, Mr. Lukic, on the Bench and we're also concerned about the witness's belief that he's going to be here for several days because that is not our understanding of the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that he just expressed his willingness to be here as long as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we have to give answers that are brief and to the point.

utterances.text: This decision could not have disrupted the relations that had been established by a piece of legislation that was of a higher level and that pertained to the entire ministry. utterances.text: Now let us look at P1044. Professor, we have seen this document a number of times during the trial here. This document comes from 1996. We see that at that period of time there was a MUP staff?

utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour, but I didn't write it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, is there something you want to add to what you said earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honours. That's all I would wish to add. I would just add that I hope that it would be a rare situation where that happens, but if it does become necessary we need to be notified before we get to court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we wonder if that should happen at all unless it's something that's cropped up and wasn't foreseen for some good reason. The report should deal with everything that the witness is going to give an opinion on, and we should not be expected to explore a wider area with the witness apart from, in our opinion, the importance of being told in advance what an expert is going to speak about and say. It does seem to us grossly unfair to any opponent to put in a report that in the main has nothing directly to do with the real issues to be addressed by the expert and then to start asking him orally to expand upon the few opinions he has expressed on the area that really matters as far as the case for this accused is concerned. So, Mr. Lukic, I hope you will make good use of the time available to you overnight to decide whether, first of all, there are parts of the report that we do not really need to admit; and secondly, to focus the questions on the important issues but confine them to what's absolutely necessary, to clarify the terms of the report on the important and relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's to deal with things that may be arisen that were not previously foreseen and that it's only right that the witness should have an opportunity to address. What we don't expect is that the real guts of your evidence will not be in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that's the case, but we'll try to tie our extra testimony with the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope -- is this the witness where at one stage the anticipated evidence in chief was going to be ten hours and that changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to imagine in this Tribunal where reports are an essential part of the presentation of the evidence of an expert that that expert -- that that witness would give evidence for anything approaching that length of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that we changed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and I assume that that is now a realistic assessment of the position, perhaps might even be generous. So with any luck we should deal with most of the evidence of this witness tomorrow. Well, Professor, we have to bring our sitting for today to an end at this stage and resume it tomorrow, which means you will have to return here to resume your evidence at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I have understood. Everything will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.
